claims.text: In as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys, magnetocaloric response and hysteresis under low applied fields are governed primarily by nanoscale structural-defect density and spatial distribution rather than composition alone.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA film has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited film displays a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transformation.
Sub-transition-temperature annealing can modify grain size and defect density without altering overall composition.
Grain boundaries and nanoscale defect sites act as distributed nucleation centers for the magnetostructural phase transition.
A higher density of grain boundaries relaxes elastic strain accumulated during the abrupt structural transformation.
Grain-boundary-mediated strain relaxation lowers the transition nucleation barrier.
A higher density of nucleation sites spreads the transformation over a broader temperature range.
Distributed nucleation smooths the magnetostructural transformation and reduces hysteresis.
Increasing grain-boundary density may enhance heat-exchange rates.
Lower defect density and larger grains reinforce an abrupt, hysteretic transition.
Annealing that reduces grain size or increases defect density will broaden the magnetocaloric transition relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing that reduces grain size or increases defect density will reduce magnetocaloric hysteresis relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Microstructure-refining annealing will improve heat-exchange properties relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The as-deposited alloy has limited heat dissipation because of a lower surface-to-volume ratio.
The predictions apply at low magnetic fields and near the intrinsic magnetostructural transition when composition remains effectively unchanged and defect density is the principal variable altered.
The quantitative relationship among defect density, transition broadening, and heat-exchange rate is not established.
Aging or other processing-induced phenomena may influence the relationship between defect density and magnetocaloric behavior.
